claims.text: The literal placeholder text 'Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported' can appear in a log line, a generated file, or a resource property when an Output is treated as if it were already a plain value.

The page at /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/output-values/ ('Output value errors') exists and provides a rundown of the 'Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported' symptom and other symptoms of treating an output as if it were already a plain value.
Resources created inside an `apply` callback will not appear in `pulumi preview` unless the output's value is already known.
Because resources created inside `apply` may not appear in `pulumi preview`, the preview output may not match the actual changes made when `pulumi up` is run.

There is a Pulumi troubleshooting guide page at /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/output-values/ that diagnoses errors from stringifying, branching on, or reading an output value like a plain value.
Stringifying, branching on, or reading a Pulumi output value like a plain value can produce diagnosable errors.

Pulumi resource properties are represented as Outputs rather than plain values because their real values are not known until the resource providing them has actually been created or updated.

If you concatenate, log, or otherwise convert a Pulumi output value to a string directly instead of going through apply or an equivalent helper, Pulumi does not raise an error by default but silently substitutes a placeholder message in place of the value.

In TypeScript, calling toString on a Pulumi Output (e.g. via string interpolation) produces a string containing the literal text 'Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported', followed by guidance to use apply or pulumi.interpolate instead, without throwing an exception.

In TypeScript, calling JSON.stringify() on a Pulumi Output, or letting one flow into a JSON body, produces a string 'Calling [toJSON] on an [Output<T>] is not supported' rather than the serialized value.

In Python, converting a Pulumi Output to a string (e.g. via an f-string) produces a broken string containing the literal text 'Calling __str__ on an Output[T] is not supported' and logs a warning, without raising an exception.
In Python, passing a Pulumi Output to json.dumps() fails outright with 'TypeError: Object of type Output is not JSON serializable'.
In Python, Output.json_dumps() should be used instead of json.dumps() to serialize a Pulumi Output to JSON.
In Go, passing a pulumi.StringOutput where a string is expected is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise, because Go's static typing generally prevents this class of mistake.
In Go, the fix for the output-to-string mistake is to resolve the value inside ApplyT and pass the result on, rather than trying to read a pulumi.StringOutput as a plain string.

In C#, calling ToString on a Pulumi Output (e.g. via string interpolation) produces a string containing the literal text 'Calling [ToString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported', followed by guidance to use Apply or Output.Format instead, without throwing an exception.

Setting the environment variable PULUMI_ERROR_OUTPUT_STRING=true, in TypeScript, Python, and C#, causes code that would otherwise silently produce a placeholder string from converting an Output to a string to instead throw an exception at the point of the mistake.
TypeScript provides pulumi.interpolate and pulumi.concat as string-composition helpers for working with outputs.
Python provides Output.concat, Output.format, and Output.json_dumps as string-composition helpers for working with outputs.
Go provides pulumi.Sprintf and pulumi.JSONMarshal as string-composition helpers for working with outputs.
C# provides Output.Format as a string-composition helper for working with outputs.

A value read out of a Pulumi output inside an apply/Apply callback is only available inside that callback (or in another output derived from it); assigning it to an outer variable and using that variable later outside the callback does not work as expected.

In the given TypeScript example, assigning the resolved bucket name to an outer variable inside bucket.bucketName.apply() leaves that outer variable still undefined when read immediately afterward, because the apply callback runs asynchronously after the rest of the program's top-level code has already finished running.
An apply callback on a Pulumi output runs when the engine resolves the dependency graph, not on a fixed timer, so the undefined-variable problem cannot be fixed by adding a delay.
Most Pulumi resource inputs accept outputs as well as plain values.
A resource's logical name is a position that cannot accept a Pulumi output value.

In a dynamically typed Pulumi SDK language, writing an if statement directly on an output object evaluates the output object itself rather than its eventual value, so the branch is generally always true regardless of what the output resolves to.
In a statically typed Pulumi SDK language, branching directly on an output (e.g. an Output<bool>) is usually a compile error because an Output<bool> is not a bool.

A plain value that is already known when a Pulumi program starts, such as a stack configuration setting read with pulumi.Config, an environment variable, or a hardcoded flag, branches on it exactly as expected with no special handling needed.

In the given TypeScript example, writing if (vpc.vpcId) does not work because the branch is evaluated on the Output object rather than its value, while deriving a new Output via vpc.vpcId.apply((id) => ...) works because it produces an Output whose value depends on the branch.

A resource's logical name (the first constructor argument) and the loop bounds or map keys used while authoring a Pulumi program must be known plain values while the program is still being evaluated, before any resource actually exists.
In TypeScript, Go, and C#, passing a Pulumi output as a resource's logical name, a loop bound, or a map key fails to compile because these positions are typed as plain strings or numbers.
In Python, passing a Pulumi output as a resource's logical name raises 'TypeError: Expected resource name to be a string' at runtime.
In Python, using a Pulumi output as a loop bound via range(some_output) raises "TypeError: 'Output' object cannot be interpreted as an integer" at runtime.

In Python, using a Pulumi output as a dictionary key does not raise an error; Python falls back to comparing and hashing the output object itself, so the lookup silently keys on the wrong thing rather than on the value the output will eventually resolve to.

If dependent resources genuinely cannot know required data until an earlier resource has been provisioned, one fix is to restructure the dependent resources into a later, separate stack that consumes the first stack's outputs through a StackReference.

Pulumi has no supported way to block a program and synchronously pull a resolved value out of an output; trying to await an output or read its value synchronously either doesn't compile, fails at runtime, or quietly returns placeholder text instead of the value.
The `pulumi stack output <name>` CLI command reads a single stack output after a deployment.
A StackReference from another Pulumi program can be used to consume one stack's outputs as another stack's inputs.

The Pulumi Automation API exposes an `outputs` field on the result of running an update (for example, `res.Outputs` in Go, or the equivalent in other languages' Automation API packages) for use when driving deployments programmatically.
